source.title: Scaling Laws for Hypernetwork-Based Knowledge Injection in Large Language Models
source.authors: Nischay Dhankhar; Dos Baha; Abulhair Saparov

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to knowledge injection: it measures answer-token loss as hypernetwork architecture, target-model size, injected-fact count, and LoRA rank vary. It does not reproduce text-pretraining scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The reported losses are for factual question answering after train-time knowledge injection, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy. The paper does not test the original parameter/token/compute allocation law or explicitly validate small-run extrapolations. Cited results from other papers are not recorded. Appendix F shows loss trajectories against training FLOPs, but does not report a fitted loss-versus-compute law.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws of answer-token cross-entropy loss after train-time knowledge injection. It varies hypernetwork width, hypernetwork depth, frozen target-model size, fact count and LoRA rank, and compares hypernetworks with LoRA and full finetuning. That bears on V5 (the power-law form in a finetuning-type regime). It does not measure pretraining loss, test extrapolation, optimise a compute split, or fit alternative functional forms to the same data.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress three points. Target-model size gives the steepest exponents of all axes. Finetuning scales slightly better in-distribution, but hypernetworks scale more steeply on all OOD splits. LoRA-rank scaling saturates, unlike the other axes. Large hypernetworks carry a large parameter overhead.
record.recipe_differences: This study scales knowledge-injection QA loss using randomly initialized hypernetworks that generate LoRA adapters, and compares with LoRA and full finetuning. It does not reproduce the original language-model pretraining loss, token-count, or compute-scaling protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling exponents vary by axis, evaluation metric, and adaptation method. OOD rephrased loss has flatter exponents than other metrics in several sweeps; LoRA rank shows a saturating curve requiring an additive constant.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling exponents differ by evaluation split: OOD rephrased is flattest on every axis. Hypernetworks have steeper OOD exponents than LoRA/full FT, while finetuning has slightly steeper ID exponents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling exponents for adaptation methods depend on the evaluation distribution and the adaptation mechanism.

record.problems: No uncertainty intervals or error bars are reported for fitted exponents. Scaling fits use a limited number of settings (five for most axes; four for full finetuning), and the 14B full-finetuning setting was not evaluated. The paper notes that the 0.5B hypernetwork target-model point lies noticeably above its fit, suggesting a capacity threshold. OOD domains have base-model accuracy approximately 4.8% above the in-distribution mean, which the authors identify as relevant to interpreting OOD results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately quantified outcomes under the 60-row limit. Appendix F loss trajectories against cumulative training FLOPs are not fitted as a compute-scaling law.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No out-of-sample prediction of larger runs. The 14B full-FT expectation is speculation only.
No compute-optimal parameter/token split. The advice to favour target size is not a fitted allocation law.
Target-model shape at fixed parameters is not varied. Hypernetwork depth/width are varied but parameter count is not held fixed for width.
Other modalities, repeated data and transfer are not tested. Ranges are about 1–1.5 orders of magnitude, not several.
No accuracy results are reported despite the abstract's mention of reasoning accuracy.
No comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting or schedules on the same law.

record.verdict_notes: V7 links are removed throughout. Exponent differences across axes and metrics are distinct laws, not evidence that fitting choices change one law. The LoRA-rank bend is treated under V5. The figure 3 legend and caption values disagree slightly, and the fixed dmodel for depth scaling (512 in the text vs 256 in Table 3) is inconsistent. Hyperparameters were set by power-law interpolation of the learning rate, which is a tool, not a result. Results are from a single preprint with no error bars.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss as a function of language-model parameters, training tokens, or training compute.
It reports fitted scaling curves but does not test predictions from fits on small runs against substantially larger runs.
It does not optimize parameter/token allocations under a fixed compute budget or test how an optimal split changes with compute.
It varies hypernetwork width and depth but does not compare target-model architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Tests scaling in one knowledge-injection setup, including finetuning comparators, but not other modalities, repeated-data training, or transfer settings generally.
The task is knowledge injection and its QA evaluation, not a test of downstream performance predictability from pretraining loss or pretraining scale.
Shows differences across scaling axes and adaptation methods, and a saturating LoRA-rank curve; does not compare alternative fitting methods or test the original compute-optimal split.

relationships.condition: Knowledge-injection QA loss vs hypernetwork width, depth, frozen target size and fact count; LoRA/full-FT loss vs target size (Qwen2.5 0.5B–14B)
relationships.reason: All sweeps give monotone log-log power-law fits (exponents −0.03 to −0.25), though over only 5–6 points spanning about 1–1.5 orders of magnitude, with no fit-quality or uncertainty reported (r1–r24).
relationships.display_finding: All sweeps yielded decreasing power-law fits with exponents from −0.03 to −0.25, using 5–6 points over approximately 1–1.5 orders of magnitude without reported fit quality or uncertainty.

relationships.reason: The authors say a pure power law fails; a large additive floor (0.54–0.80) is needed (r25–r28).
relationships.display_finding: A pure power law failed to describe LoRA-rank scaling, requiring an additive floor of 0.54–0.80.

relationships.condition: Smallest frozen target (0.5B) under hypernetwork injection
relationships.reason: The text states the 0.5B point lies noticeably above the target-size fit, suggesting a capacity threshold (r9).
relationships.display_finding: The 0.5B target lay noticeably above the target-size fit, suggesting a capacity threshold.
